newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks to tighten grip on Ohio, Pennsylvania.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks to tighten grip on Ohio, Pennsylvania.

text.p: Sounding confident and feisty with one week to Election Day, President Bill Clinton on Tuesday worked to tighten his grip on the American heartland by campaigning in Ohio and Pennsylvania.

Speaking in the morning to several thousand students at Ohio State University in Columbus, Clinton jokingly brushed off about a dozen supporters of Republican Bob Dole who heckled him with shouts of "Dole-Kemp" and "Tell the truth."

"I bet you they won't be doing that a week from today," he said, prompting laughter and cheers. "They must not have any student loans -- Senator Dole voted against creating the student loan programme."

"I would be screaming too if I wanted a country that took Head Start and Big Bird away from five year-olds, school lunches away from 10 year-olds, summer jobs away from 15 year-olds and college loans away from 20 year-olds," he said.

The Head Start programme, which helps poor young children learn to read and write, was expanded under Clinton in May 1994 when he signed a bill to increase funding by $700 million, to $4 billion. Big Bird is a popular character on educational television.

"We are not afraid of honest discussion and debate, so we don't have to shout our opponents down," he added. "But I might be screaming if I had that kind of record, either that or running and looking for a rock to hide behind."

Despite his commanding lead and his own buoyant confidence, Clinton's appearances in Ohio and Pennsylvania signalled that he has no intention of neglecting the country's pivotal swing states as he starts the final sprint to the Nov. 5 election.
"We got some juice in the audience," he said happily after his speech at Ohio State's basketball arena. "That was great."
Speaking in Columbus, Clinton offered some modest proposals to improve educational standards, all at little or no cost to the federal government:
-- urging states to issue "report cards" on public schools to allow parents to better judge their performance;
-- calling on states to have clear, tough standards in order to promote students from one grade to the next;
-- and encouraging the creation of more "charter schools," which are run by parents and teachers.
After the Columbus rally, Clinton stopped at the Immaculate Conception Catholic grade school in the town of Clintonville to shake hands with dozens of delighted children.
Later at a big outdoor rally at Philadelphia's University of Pennsylvania, he said: "We have to raise standards, define them, expect them, measure them and hold people accountable."

All national opinion polls show Clinton holds an imposing lead over Dole one week from the election, with the latest CNN USA Today Gallup tracking poll putting it at 13 percentage points and the latest Reuters survey at 12.6 points.
As a result, Clinton has recently had the luxury of campaigning in states that he does not need to win and has begun "leaning away" from parts of the country where his support was strong, aides said.
But in Ohio and Pennsylvania, Clinton was courting states where elections are often won and lost.

In Ohio, Clinton has 14-point lead over Dole according to an Oct. 17-19 Cincinnati Enquirer poll, while in Pennsylvania the picture was even brighter according to an Oct. 13-15 Mason-Dixon survey, which gave him a 15-point lead there.

Clinton was scheduled to fly back to Washington on Tuesday afternoon, spending one night in the White House before setting off on Wednesday on a seven-day burst of travel that will bring him to Little Rock, Arkansas on election night.
